lead: A MOSFET does not obey Ohm's law. Above threshold the gate sets the channel charge and the drain voltage pulls that charge along. Two square-law formulas follow — one for the linear region, one for saturation — giving drain current from the gate overdrive and the W/L ratio. Designers use them to size transistors, estimate gain and find on-resistance before running a simulator.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for the three regions and 1.2 for VT.

sections.h3: Channel charge and the drift integral

blocks.text: Take an nMOS with the source at 0 V. Let x run from 0 at the source to L at the drain, where L is the channel length in metres. Let V(x) be the channel potential, so V(0) = 0 and V(L) = V<sub>DS</sub>. The oxide capacitance per unit area is C<sub>ox</sub> = ε<sub>ox</sub>/t<sub>ox</sub> in F/m², with ε<sub>ox</sub> the oxide permittivity and t<sub>ox</sub> the oxide thickness. Above threshold the inversion charge per unit area at x is Q(x) = C<sub>ox</sub>[V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> − V(x)] in C/m². V<sub>GS</sub> is gate-to-source voltage, V<sub>T</sub> is threshold voltage, and V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> is the overdrive V<sub>ov</sub>.

An electron drifts with velocity v = µ<sub>n</sub>E, where µ<sub>n</sub> is electron mobility in m²/(V·s) and E = dV/dx is the lateral field. Current is charge per unit length times velocity: I<sub>D</sub> = WQ(x)v, where W is channel width in metres. Substituting, I<sub>D</sub> = Wµ<sub>n</sub>C<sub>ox</sub>[V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> − V(x)]dV/dx. I<sub>D</sub> is the same at every x, since the channel stores no net charge in steady state.

Separate and integrate from source to drain. The left side gives I<sub>D</sub>L; the right side gives Wµ<sub>n</sub>C<sub>ox</sub>[(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>)V<sub>DS</sub> − V<sub>DS</sub>²/2]. Divide by L and write k<sub>n</sub>′ = µ<sub>n</sub>C<sub>ox</sub>.

blocks.where: valid for V<sub>DS</sub> ≤ V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> (that is, V<sub>DS</sub> ≤ V<sub>ov</sub>); k<sub>n</sub>′ = µ<sub>n</sub>C<sub>ox</sub> in A/V²; W/L is the width-to-length ratio; V<sub>GS</sub>, V<sub>DS</sub> and V<sub>T</sub> are in volts; I<sub>D</sub> is in amperes.

blocks.text: At V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>ov</sub> the charge at the drain end falls to zero, Q(L) = 0, and the channel is pinched off. Beyond that point the extra drain voltage drops across a short depleted region near the drain, not across the conducting channel, so the current stays almost constant. Put V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>ov</sub> in the linear formula: the bracket becomes V<sub>ov</sub>² − V<sub>ov</sub>²/2 = V<sub>ov</sub>²/2.

blocks.where: valid for V<sub>DS</sub> ≥ V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>; the factor ½ belongs to saturation; k<sub>n</sub>′ = µ<sub>n</sub>C<sub>ox</sub> in A/V²; W/L is dimensionless; I<sub>D</sub> is in amperes.

blocks.text: The transfer characteristic plots I<sub>D</sub> against V<sub>GS</sub> at fixed V<sub>DS</sub>: zero for V<sub>GS</sub> ≤ V<sub>T</sub>, then rising as (V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>)². The output family plots I<sub>D</sub> against V<sub>DS</sub> for several V<sub>GS</sub>; each curve rises almost linearly, bends near V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>ov</sub> and flattens. The figure uses k<sub>n</sub>′ = 1 mA/V², W/L = 1 and V<sub>T</sub> = 0.5 V. At V<sub>GS</sub> = 2.0 V the overdrive is 1.5 V, so the flat current is ½ × 1 mA/V² × 1 × (1.5 V)² = 1.125 mA. At V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.5 V it is 0.5 mA; at V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.0 V it is 0.125 mA.

Some syllabi call these the square-law equations, the Shichman-Hodges model or SPICE Level-1. The pMOS has the same shape with all signs flipped: use V<sub>SG</sub> = V<sub>S</sub> − V<sub>G</sub>, V<sub>SD</sub> = V<sub>S</sub> − V<sub>D</sub> and |V<sub>T</sub>|. Saturation: I<sub>D</sub> = ½ k<sub>p</sub>′(W/L)(V<sub>SG</sub> − |V<sub>T</sub>|)². Linear: I<sub>D</sub> = k<sub>p</sub>′(W/L)[(V<sub>SG</sub> − |V<sub>T</sub>|)V<sub>SD</sub> − V<sub>SD</sub>²/2], with k<sub>p</sub>′ = µ<sub>p</sub>C<sub>ox</sub>. In many processes µ<sub>p</sub> is about 0.25 to 0.5 times µ<sub>n</sub>, so a pMOS of the same W/L is weaker and is made wider.

The transconductance g<sub>m</sub> is the change in I<sub>D</sub> for a small change in V<sub>GS</sub> at fixed V<sub>DS</sub>. Differentiating the square law: g<sub>m</sub> = k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>), which is also g<sub>m</sub> = 2I<sub>D</sub>/(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>). Units are A/V, also called siemens (S). A larger overdrive or larger W/L gives more gain per volt.

Near V<sub>DS</sub> = 0 the transistor acts as a resistor. Differentiating the linear formula at V<sub>DS</sub> = 0 gives the slope k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>); the on-resistance is its inverse, R<sub>on</sub> ≈ 1/[k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>)]. This is the resistance of a closed switch. It falls as the overdrive or W/L rises, which is why a gate driven at a higher supply makes a faster switch.

Rearranged for design, saturation gives W/L = 2ID/[kn′(VGS − VT)²]. In a current mirror the ratio of W/L sets the ratio of currents. In a digital gate the on-resistance and the load capacitance set the delay; see 1.5. Channel-length modulation and velocity saturation are ignored here; their corrections are in 1.4.

figure.caption: Output characteristics for k<sub>n</sub>′ = 1 mA/V², W/L = 1 and V<sub>T</sub> = 0.5 V. Each curve is linear at low V<sub>DS</sub> and flat once V<sub>DS</sub> reaches the overdrive; the flat level follows the square law.

spec.aria: Output characteristics of a square-law nMOS with 1 mA/V² gain and 0.5 V threshold, each curve rising linearly then flattening at the saturation current for its gate overdrive.

examples.question: An nMOS has k<sub>n</sub>′ = 100 µA/V², W/L = 20, V<sub>T</sub> = 0.5 V, V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.5 V and V<sub>DS</sub> = 2 V. Find the drain current and transconductance. Then find the drain current with the same gate voltage when V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.5 V.
steps: Overdrive: V<sub>ov</sub> = V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> = 1.5 V − 0.5 V = 1.0 V.
V<sub>DS</sub> = 2 V ≥ V<sub>ov</sub> = 1.0 V, so the device is in saturation.
I<sub>D</sub> = ½ k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)V<sub>ov</sub>² = 0.5 × 100 µA/V² × 20 × (1.0 V)² = 1000 µA = 1 mA.
g<sub>m</sub> = k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)V<sub>ov</sub> = 100 µA/V² × 20 × 1.0 V = 2000 µA/V = 2 mA/V.
At V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.5 V < 1.0 V the device is in the linear region.
I<sub>D</sub> = k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)[V<sub>ov</sub>V<sub>DS</sub> − V<sub>DS</sub>²/2] = 100 µA/V² × 20 × [(1.0 V)(0.5 V) − (0.5 V)²/2] = 2000 µA/V² × 0.375 V² = 750 µA = 0.75 mA.
examples.answer: The device carries I<sub>D</sub> = 1 mA in saturation, its transconductance is g<sub>m</sub> = 2 mA/V, and at V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.5 V in the linear region it carries 0.75 mA.
examples.check:
kn = 100e-6
wl = 20
vt = 0.5
vgs = 1.5
vds = 2.0
vov = vgs - vt
idsat = 0.5 * kn * wl * vov**2
gm = kn * wl * vov
vds2 = 0.5
idlin = kn * wl * (vov * vds2 - vds2**2 / 2)
print(idsat * 1e3)
print(gm * 1e3)
print(idlin * 1e3)

traps: Putting V<sub>DS</sub> into the saturation formula in place of the overdrive (V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>), which makes the current keep growing after saturation.
Dropping the factor ½ in the saturation formula, which doubles every saturation answer.
Writing L/W where the formula needs W/L, which is easy to do when rearranging for a given current.
Treating a pMOS as an nMOS with a positive V<sub>T</sub>; flip the signs and use V<sub>SG</sub>, V<sub>SD</sub> and |V<sub>T</sub>|.

quiz.q: State the saturation condition and the saturation drain-current formula for an nMOS.
quiz.a: Saturation holds when V<sub>DS</sub> ≥ V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>. Then I<sub>D</sub> = ½ k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>)².

quiz.q: Why does the drain current flatten after V<sub>DS</sub> reaches the overdrive?
quiz.a: At V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> the inversion charge at the drain end falls to zero and the channel is pinched off. Extra drain voltage drops across a short depleted region near the drain, so it does not add charge to the conducting channel. The current therefore stays almost constant.

quiz.q: Write the on-resistance formula near V<sub>DS</sub> = 0 and explain why a higher V<sub>GS</sub> lowers it.
quiz.a: R<sub>on</sub> ≈ 1/[k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>)]. A higher V<sub>GS</sub> raises the overdrive and hence the channel charge, so the I<sub>D</sub>–V<sub>DS</sub> slope at the origin grows. The inverse of that slope is smaller, so R<sub>on</sub> falls.

quiz.q: An nMOS has k<sub>n</sub>′ = 50 µA/V², W/L = 10, V<sub>T</sub> = 0.4 V, V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.4 V and V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.3 V. Find I<sub>D</sub>.
quiz.a: V<sub>ov</sub> = 1.4 V − 0.4 V = 1.0 V. Since V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.3 V ≤ 1.0 V, the device is in the linear region. I<sub>D</sub> = 50 µA/V² × 10 × [(1.0 V)(0.3 V) − (0.3 V)²/2] = 500 µA/V² × (0.3 − 0.045) V² = 127.5 µA.

quiz.q: For the same nMOS (k<sub>n</sub>′ = 50 µA/V², W/L = 10, V<sub>T</sub> = 0.4 V, V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.4 V), find I<sub>D</sub> and g<sub>m</sub> at V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.5 V.
quiz.a: V<sub>ov</sub> = 1.0 V and V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.5 V ≥ 1.0 V, so the device is saturated. I<sub>D</sub> = ½ × 50 µA/V² × 10 × (1.0 V)² = 250 µA. g<sub>m</sub> = 50 µA/V² × 10 × 1.0 V = 500 µA/V = 0.5 mA/V.

quiz.q: A transistor must carry a fixed saturation current. If W/L is doubled, what happens to the required overdrive?
quiz.a: From I<sub>D</sub> = ½ k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L)V<sub>ov</sub>², doubling W/L halves V<sub>ov</sub>². The overdrive falls by a factor of √2, to about 0.707 of its old value.

quiz.q: Why is a pMOS weaker than an nMOS of the same W/L, and how is this fixed in design?
quiz.a: Hole mobility µ<sub>p</sub> is lower than electron mobility µ<sub>n</sub>, often about 0.25 to 0.5 times µ<sub>n</sub>, so k<sub>p</sub>′ is lower for the same C<sub>ox</sub>. A pMOS is made wider to raise W/L and match the current or resistance of the nMOS.

beyond: Not for the exam. Simulators use BSIM or EKV with dozens of parameters; the square law is the hand-analysis first pass. Low-power analog design often uses the g<sub>m</sub>/I<sub>D</sub> method instead, because it still works in weak and moderate inversion where the square law fails.
